DUBAI, Nov 2 : Abu Dhabi's ADNOC and artificial intelligence firm G42 on Monday signed a deal with OpenAI under which the state energy firm will integrate advanced AI capabilities across its operations, the Abu Dhabi Media Office said. The deal was signed as the ChatGPT maker's CEO Sam Altman met with Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi and attended the United Arab Emirates' biggest oil show, ADIPEC.  US oil firms ExxonMobil and Chevron last week cancelled plans for their executives to travel to the Gulf country and join the event, citing security concerns. Fears of fresh US attacks on Iran and retaliatory strikes by Tehran have gripped the oil markets in recent days.  US President Donald Trump has said he would not launch an attack on Iran before the US midterm elections on November 3, but on Friday he said Washington may carry out another military operation against Iran.

Source: Reuters

TOKYO, Nov 2 : Japan has made gradual progress towards anchoring inflation around the central bank's 2 per cent target, the Bank of Japan said in a report on Monday, bolstering the case for raising interest rates. In reaching its decision, the BOJ weighed up inflation expectations, firms' wage- and price-setting behaviour, and the degree to which households and firms act based on the assumption that prices will rise by around 2 per cent, the central bank said. "With underlying inflation moving around 2 per cent and upside risks to prices warranting attention, interest rate hikes will likely alleviate price pressures and underpin consumption," the bank said in the full version of its quarterly outlook. Firms' inflation outlook appears to gradually converge around 2 per cent, while households' inflation expectations vary widely, it added.

"In recent years, the share of wage increases at levels broadly consistent with 2 per cent increase plus labor productivity growth has risen," the bank added. "As such, underlying inflation has risen toward a level around 2 per cent over the past few years, and there has been gradual progress toward anchoring it at that level." Domestic consumption has recently been sluggish in real terms, the bank added, due to bad weather during the summer and a hit to spending from rising living costs. "But consumption as a whole is likely to remain resilient" partly thanks to government subsidies to curb fuel prices, higher stock prices and rising wages from a tight job market, it said. The BOJ publishes the full version of its quarterly report on the market day after it concludes its policy meeting, at which it releases a summary.

HONG KONG: HSBC is setting up an artificial intelligence and emerging technology institute in Hong Kong, as the city's largest bank steps up its AI push following a similar launch in Singapore earlier this year .  The bank aims to launch the institute in the first quarter of 2027, Chief Executive Georges Elhedery said at Hong Kong's Fintech Week event on Monday (Nov 2). The AI unit will work with Hong Kong University of Science and Technology as its anchor academic partner, Elhedery said, though he did not disclose headcount details. He added the bank would move the centre to Hong Kong's Northern Metropolis - a mega project bordering China - as soon as its site there was ready.

The Hong Kong plan follows the Asia-focused lender's announcement in July that it would hire more than 100 artificial intelligence specialists at an AI centre in rival financial hub Singapore.  The investment in AI transformation comes as banks globally cut staff due to AI-driven overhauls, with lenders such as Citi, Standard Chartered, and Barclays unveiling plans this year to cut thousands of jobs. About 80 per cent of all banks in Hong Kong are already adopting AI or generative AI, Eddie Yue, chief executive of Hong Kong's de facto central bank, told the conference.

HSBC's Elhedery added that HSBC - one of Hong Kong's largest private-sector employers with 28,000 local staff - was rolling out AI training for its entire global workforce of roughly 200,000 people. "AI is going to be disruptive. It's going to transform jobs," Elhedery said. Separately, Yue told reporters on the sidelines of the event that the regulator would launch Project SAGE to support the use of AI agents in finance while setting guardrails to manage risks. The HKMA will create a cross-sector expert panel to test AI agent applications and interoperability, Yue said.  He added that the HKMA would also seek views on governance, accountability, a central register of trusted agents and a possible "know your agent" standard. "Innovation and risk management must go hand in hand," Yue said. The HKMA will expand trials of tokenised Exchange Fund Bills and examine whether regulated stablecoins can serve as a payment method, he added.

Source: Reuters/lk

FAST

Nov 2 : John Ternus will host his first earnings call as Apple's CEO on Monday, with investors looking to the company's forecast to determine whether a blitz of new products can help offset rising costs for memory chips. Ternus, who took the reins from Tim Cook in September, has overseen the introduction of Apple's first foldable phone, smart home hub and Apple's first touch-screen laptops. All of those products began shipping during the company's current fiscal first quarter, amid what Cook had called a "100-year flood" of rising memory costs. Apple will face scrutiny over three key issues: its crucial holiday-quarter outlook, Ternus' remarks on AI and the revamped Siri, and rising memory-chip costs that analysts expect to drag quarterly profit growth to its weakest in six quarters. Apple has been trying to position its AI offerings differently than rivals such as Meta Platforms' Muse agent, which took App Store rankings by storm in recent weeks.

Rivals such as OpenAI, which Apple is suing over alleged trade-secret theft, are also developing devices aimed at displacing the iPhone as the central device in people's lives. How Apple embraces AI could also have large implications for the future of its services business, whose slowing growth has worried investors after years of rapid expansion. "Recent agentic innovation far outpaces our experience with Siri AI, but Apple has acknowledged that Siri AI ... is far more focused on trust/privacy," said Dan Morgan, portfolio manager at Synovus Trust, which owns Apple shares. Apple is marketing Apple's AI systems toward "everyday people" rather than Silicon Valley insiders, who are big users of frontier AI models from the likes of OpenAI. Morgan added that investors want to know whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through its App Store and taking a cut of the business they generate. SHARES OUTPERFORM For now, Apple's reluctance to join the massive AI spending race has worked in its favor. Its shares have risen about 27 per cent this year, outperforming tech giants such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon as investors seek shelter from mounting concerns over the cost of building AI infrastructure. Analysts expect Apple to report a nearly 11 per cent rise in revenue to $113.39 billion for the July-September period, the company's fiscal fourth quarter, according to LSEG data. Net profit is expected to rise about 6 per cent to $29.04 billion. Apple's services business is expected to grow almost 10 per cent to $31.56 billion, its slowest pace in more than three years. IPhone sales are projected to climb about 15 per cent to $56.54 billion, slowing from growth of about 22 per cent in the previous three months. The results will capture just nine days of sales of the new iPhone 18 Pro models, while the iPhone Duo, the firm's first foldable, came out on October 23, which will benefit the holiday quarter. Remarks on how the Duo is selling will be scrutinized after some buyers of the device that starts at $1,999 in the US have reported cracks and lines along the inner display's central fold, prompting Apple to offer replacements. Duo's online orders had sold out within minutes. IDC analyst Nabila Popal said she expects demand for the Duo to continue exceeding supply despite the screen problems. The test will be how quickly Apple can replace affected devices while supplies remain tight, she said. Bank of America estimates Duo buyers face average delivery waits of 79 days, with shipments stretching into January.

Source: Reuters

HONG KONG: Asian stocks were mixed on Monday (Nov 2) as investors struggled to recover from last week's tough run fuelled by disappointing earnings from tech titans, while eyes were also turning to the United States ahead of crucial midterm elections. Traders did get some support from a drop in oil prices following a report that US President Donald Trump wanted negotiations with Iran to play out rather than resume his war after the polls. Artificial intelligence (AI)-linked firms were hit by another wave of selling as Wall Street giants including Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft signalled they would keep pouring money into data centres and chips even as investors grow impatient for returns. The firms, along with Meta, are on track to spend more than US$700 billion on capital investment this year, much of it on AI infrastructure, according to analyst estimates.

The reports added to concerns that the vast sum poured into the sector may have been overdone, while Bloomberg said 90 per cent of software companies in the S&P 500 had beaten earnings expectations this season, while just 70 per cent topped revenue. That compared with all companies beating profits in the previous three months, and more than 80 per cent topping on sales. Apple, Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir are due to report this week. Steep losses in New York saw the Nasdaq end almost three per cent down, and Asian tech also struggled at the start of this week. Japanese chipmaker Kioxia plunged more than 15 per cent after giving a cautious outlook that fell short of forecasts. The firm has plunged around 70 per cent from its record high set in June, though it is still up more than 200 per cent since the start of the year. South Korea's Samsung also fell more than one per cent, though rival SK hynix was up more than one per cent. Taiwan's TSMC added nearly two per cent. The mixed performance in tech was reflected in broader markets, with Tokyo, Sydney, Singapore and Taipei all down while Seoul, Hong Kong and Shanghai rose. Oil prices sank more than two per cent on hopes for a negotiated end to the Iran crisis, with Axios reporting that the US president wanted talks to continue, to the disappointment of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The news outlet also said Vice-President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks, marking the highest-level move in months. "Despite the stalemate outcome following the Israeli elections, the chances of a diplomatic breakthrough may be improving following intensified mediation efforts by Qatar and regional allies," said FOREX.com's Razan Hilal. "Reports point to discussions about sanctions relief and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while nuclear restrictions and inspections remain major unresolved issues." However, Trump continued to hint at more military action while on the campaign trail Sunday. He reiterated his threat to resume strikes, telling a rally: "The only reason why I'm not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. "I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we're going to have to give them the hammer." That came after he had told reporters that "we still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes". For its part, Iran's army spokesman Mohammad Akramini said at the weekend that any renewed war could last longer than the previous round of fighting, and that "the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion". Investors were keeping tabs on the midterms, where Democrats are predicted to see thumping wins as they look to take back control of Congress and impose a first political check on Trump's unprecedented pursuit of power. Polls show Democrats are all but certain to take the majority from Republicans in the House of Representatives in Tuesday's vote and have a shot at winning the Senate.

FAST

SYDNEY, Nov 2 : Share markets steadied in Asia on Monday as investors hoped for Apple earnings later in the day to provide some relief from AI cash-burn worries, while oil prices eased after talks continued between Iranian and Qatari mediators. Apple has been an oasis of relative calm given it does not spend billions on data centres, and its shares have climbed for four months straight to help it unseat Nvidia as the world's most valuable listed company. Analysts are looking for quarterly earnings per share (EPS) of $2 on revenue of $113 billion, up from $1.85 the same time last year. The company might also offer some guidance on how early sales of the iPhone 18 are performing with pre-orders having started in mid-October. The optimism helped S&P 500 futures edge up 0.4 per cent, while Nasdaq futures bounced 0.8 per cent. The tech-heavy Nasdaq lost almost 7 per cent in October for its worst month since the 'Liberation Day' tariff rout of April 2025.

Some upbeat news is sorely needed after concerns about negative cash flow and the sheer scale of AI capex saw the cost of insuring against corporate defaults blow out last week. Intel's near 29 per cent tumble on Friday has also raised the stakes for other chip groups, including AMD. An added wrinkle is the midterm elections in the United States, where a win by Democrats in either or both houses could result in more political hurdles for data centres. Analysts at Goldman Sachs expect capex by hyperscalers to almost double to $800 billion this year, and rise further to $1.2 trillion in 2027. At the same time, they see S&P 500 EPS growth of nearly 30 per cent in 2026 slowing to 18 per cent next year. "Earnings results have underscored the fundamental challenge facing equity investors — earnings growth is strong, but it is no longer accelerating," wrote Ben Snider, Goldman's chief US equity strategist, in a note. "Similarly, Q3 results support our view that AI investment spending will continue to grow but that the growth rate of AI capex is peaking." Adding to the air of unease were withdrawals from Binance as the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange went back online on Sunday after hackers stole billions from the platform last week. Japan's Nikkei was down 0.1 per cent, but off early lows, while South Korea added 0.8 per cent, having shed 16 per cent last month. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.2 per cent. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures and DAX futures both firmed 0.1 per cent, while FTSE futures were flat.  MORE RATE HIKES COMING The retreat in equities last month provided a reprieve to safe-haven bonds, with investors wondering if a sustained selloff in the stock market could deter the Federal Reserve from hiking interest rates in December. Futures still imply a 72 per cent chance of a quarter-point rate rise, but now only have 55 basis points of total tightening priced in compared to more than 70 basis points a month ago. Yields on 10-year Treasuries nudged up to 4.941 per cent, but remained well off their October peak of 5.3645 per cent, while 2-year yields stood at 4.612 per cent. Among central banks meeting this week, markets are wagering on hikes from the Reserve Bank of Australia, Bank of England and Riksbank, while the Norges Bank is seen on hold. Economic data due this week includes the influential US ISM survey of manufacturing for October later on Monday, while the all-important payrolls report is on Friday. Median forecasts are for a 65,000 rise in jobs, after September's disappointing 29,000 gain, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.2 per cent. In currency markets, the majors were pretty much sidelined while all the action was concentrated in stocks. The euro was a shade firmer at $1.1169, while the dollar was barely changed at 157.75 yen. For commodities, oil prices slipped as talks continued aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, though tankers were still being attacked in the Gulf. Brent futures dipped 2.0 per cent to $111.15 a barrel, though that follows a 13.6 per cent jump in October, while US crude futures eased 2.3 per cent to $101.73 a barrel. Non-interest-bearing gold bounced 0.9 per cent to $3,911 an ounce, having fallen 6.8 per cent last month amid talk some investors were having to sell to cover margin calls on equities. [GOL/]

DARWIN/SYDNEY, Nov 2 : The developer of one of Australia's biggest planned data centres scrapped its target start date after a regulator said it needed longer than usual to set environmental parameters, a setback to the country's ambitions to be a fast-track destination for AI investment. Startup Energy North, which says it has finance lined up for a sprawling gas and solar-powered data centre on a cattle ranch in the country's remote north, 683 km (424 miles) from the nearest city, had given a "first power" date of June 28, 2028, in regulatory filings four months ago. But after the Northern Territory environment regulator said in an October 7 ruling it was suspending its seven-week deadline to decide what hurdles the project must clear, the developer told Reuters it had scrubbed its timeline. "The June 2028 date in our referral was an indicative schedule at the time of lodgement, and we're no longer working to it," said Energy North vice president of project development Daniel Hunter in an email.

The project is the biggest in Australia to put back its timing and shows how data centre ambitions face hurdles even in the isolated north, which has sought to differentiate itself from cities in the contest for the $7 trillion McKinsey forecasts will be invested in "AI factories" globally by 2030. The Territory is counting on luring projects with its vast supply of uninhabited land and sunshine — 260,000 residents in an area twice the size of Texas, with as much sun as the Sahara — and a huge just-opened shale gas reserve for backup power. But stopping the clock on Energy North, the Territory's regulator said it would seek advice from the federal government, which is "developing policy expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure developers", and gave no new timeframe. Hunter said the project was unfazed and would confirm timing once the regulator sets out terms for an environmental impact statement, required to identify and address potential adverse effects. He declined to say who is lined up to finance the project. ISOLATED TERRITORY NOT IMMUNE TO PUSHBACK At 1 gigawatt, Energy North's "Project Ares" is four times the size of a data centre expansion in Melbourne delayed this month by developer NextDC due to energy supply concerns and 10 times the size of a project pulled by Goodman in Sydney amid resident pushback. "Our antiquated planning frameworks weren't designed for proposals like this," said Adam Beck, an urban planner who has written environmental impact statements for infrastructure projects and advises governments. "Tearing up timelines is kind of standard process, but I'm not going to discount the lack of social license. There is a certain heightened level of concern by the community, and that's playing out on real projects." In its ruling on Energy North's proposed 191 sq km (74 sq mile) data centre campus, including a gas turbine system, solar farm, airstrip and accommodation for 4,300 construction workers, the Territory's Environment Protection Agency warned of 10 impacts, from straining water systems to disrupting Aboriginal sacred sites. It said it had a "low level of confidence in the effectiveness of proposed measures to manage potential significant impact". Northern Territory business minister Robyn Cahill, who has said her government was talking to 12 data centre-related projects, didn't respond to requests for comment. FEASIBILITY IN FOCUS The gap between hope and reality isn't limited to Energy North's project. Beetaloo Energy has proposed a data centre near Darwin, twice the size of Project Ares. It would use up to 400 terajoules of gas a day, based on an estimate it gave of needing 200 terajoules per gigawatt. That is 10 times the volume of gas flowing from the Beetaloo Basin's only producing project, Tamboran's Shenandoah South. Beetaloo Energy aims to start producing a small volume by year-end. Just those two data centres would total 3 gigawatts, about 10 times peak demand on the entire Territory's grid. Both companies said their energy would ultimately combine renewables with their own gas-fired power, bypassing the grid. Details of the other 10 Territory projects haven't been disclosed. Aboriginal consultation in a territory where a quarter of the population is Indigenous, meanwhile, needs travel, interpreters and repeat visits, and expediting it "does not produce prompt consent", Aboriginal group the Northern Land Council said in a submission to an ongoing federal inquiry. The Northern Territory Cattlemen's Association expected data centre development with "effective regulation, properly enforced, that safeguards pastoral operations and the land, water and environment both industries depend on", said CEO Romy Carey. The Territory government can override stakeholder objections but not when a complaint goes to the federal or High Court, said Rolf Gerritsen, a former policy head for the Territory chief minister's office who teaches at Charles Darwin University. "If you've got increased opposition groups ... whatever the development proposal is, it does tend to tie it up," he said.

Source: Reuters

LONDON/MOSCOW, Nov 1 : OPEC+ oil-producing countries kept December production targets steady on Sunday, confirming expectations that more policy adjustments will not occur until next year, as the group continues to struggle with export disruptions from the Iran war. Seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — made the decision in an online meeting on Sunday, OPEC said in a statement. While Gulf members have been boosting exports that have been disrupted for months by the conflict, most are still pumping well below their targets. OPEC+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia. Only the seven members — plus the United Arab Emirates until it quit OPEC in May — have been involved in monthly output decisions in recent years. All members of the 21-country group are due to meet on November 29, when analysts expect it will decide 2027 quotas. "Today's decision was the easy one," said Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad. "The much more important test comes at the November 29 ministerial meeting, when OPEC+ will decide its 2027 production framework."

Oil prices jumped more than 2 per cent on Friday, with Brent crude settling at almost $118 a barrel, the highest since April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in the Iran war after the US midterm elections. The International Energy Agency and other forecasters have warned of excess supply in 2027 should Gulf flows return to normal. "OPEC+ faces an extremely difficult call for 2027," Leon added. "The group has to plan around huge uncertainty over the US-Iran war, the pace of recovery through the Strait of Hormuz, and the size of the surplus that could emerge once disrupted barrels return." OIL CAPACITY REVIEW IN FOCUS The seven members have been boosting output targets for much of 2026 and in September completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. At earlier meetings, they kept the targets steady for October and November. OPEC+ still has one more layer of production cuts of about 2 million bpd covering most members through the end of 2026. The group needs to complete a review of members' production capacity during the fourth quarter before setting the 2027 baselines that will determine future quotas and shape plans to unwind those cuts, sources have said. The Iran war has disrupted projects to expand capacity across the Middle East, throwing estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, Reuters reported in October. As a result, the review is now expected to be completed by mid-November. (Writing by Alex Lawler; Editing by Joe Bavier and Alex Richardson)

Exports from Asia's fourth-largest economy, a bellwether for global trade, rose 93.7 per cent last month to $115.28 billion, slightly higher than a median 93.2 per cent rise forecast in a Reuters poll of economists. Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, resumed bitcoin, ether and some stablecoin withdrawals on Sunday (Nov 1) and said others would follow in phases, after it covered 95 per cent of the US$6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform. The heist, which the FBI has tied to North Korea and analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole US$2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. Binance, which was founded in China, said the first phase of withdrawals would cover 15 crypto assets including bitcoin, ether, XRP and dogecoin. Bitcoin withdrawals resumed shortly after 0600 GMT, while ether, BNB and some USDT and USDC stablecoin withdrawals were also restored. Binance said it had covered US$6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5 per cent of stolen tokens consist of assets that are less liquid and may take longer to source in the required amounts, according to the exchange. FBI TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNIT

The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment. Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Analysts had also blamed North Korea for the heist. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. US President Donald Trump, however, said on Saturday that the United States was still not certain if North Korea was involved. "We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters on Saturday in comments posted by a White House account on X.

Related:

Gone in 20 minutes: How the biggest heist in crypto history unfolded

BINANCE VOWS TO BEAR FINANCIAL COSTS Binance has been working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about US$3 billion located as of Friday, it said. The exchange has repeatedly said it would bear the financial impact of the funds stolen in the hack. It has set aside around US$6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance's US$1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X. Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that 50 per cent of its SAFU funds would be used, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about US$1 billion. Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after the hack. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about US$162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report. BINANCE FOUNDER CZ THANKS US LAW ENFORCEMENT In a post on X that quoted the FBI statement on North Korea’s involvement, Binance thanked the agency for its support. It did not respond to a request for comment on North Korea's involvement. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who was convicted in the US of failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program before being pardoned by Trump last year, said US law enforcement agencies provided vital help, including by tracking and freezing the stolen assets. "A tweet can't fully express our gratitude. Many crypto bros may not realize, a lot of the 'why bitcoin didn't drop more?' credit goes to them," Zhao wrote, referring to the US law enforcement agencies.

Related:

Hackers allegedly from North Korea steal US$6.3 billion from Binance in world's biggest crypto heist

Oct 31 : Crypto exchange Binance said on Saturday it has been able to replace 90 per cent of the amount stolen after a record $6.3 billion hack of its platform by using company money to buy new tokens. The remaining 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90 per cent of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10 per cent. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X on Saturday.  Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after losing more than $6 billion worth of crypto in a hack that analysts and the FBI blamed on North Korea.

The FBI on Saturday said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology.  Teng said on Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said on Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday. Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses.  The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT on October 31, as part of its proof-of-reserves process. Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.

NEW YORK, Oct 31 : US electricity prices had flown under the radar in past national elections, but they have become a major political issue in this year's midterms as Americans grow angry over rising utility bills and deals for power-hungry data centers. Nationwide, according to Energy Information Administration data, electricity prices for homes have risen more than 10 per cent since 2024 when President Donald Trump was elected along with Republican majorities in both houses of the US Congress. Higher electricity prices have outpaced the rise in costs for other goods and services. Power bills have grown even faster in political battleground states of Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania, which are also hot spots for new data centers. In some cases, electricity bills have soared by triple the inflation rate.  Many politicians vying for top statehouse seats across the country this year have backed cracking down on utilities. Some have proposed freezing utility rate increases and slashing guaranteed returns, steps that could have sweeping consequences for the country's utility industry.

"It could be the first election to feature utilities and electricity, specifically, as a prominent issue in the midterms," said Charles Hua, executive director of PowerLines, a nonprofit that advocates reforming utility policy to favor consumers. "Part of that is because people's utility bills have gone up and up, and they don't see any end in sight."  Utilities are heavily regulated. State regulators generally must approve utilities’ requests to spend on the grid and to recover those costs through rate increases. Regulators also set the return on equity utilities can earn on their grid investments.  This year, utilities are on track to match last year's record high $31 billion in rate increase requests to regulators, a PowerLines survey showed.  Last year's spending was double the previous record. The investor-owned companies are also expected to carry out a record of nearly $1.3 trillion in capital spending over the next five years, according to an analysis by S&P Global’s Regulatory Research Associates. UTILITIES SPOTLIGHTED Seats on nine state public utility commissions are up for election this year, nearly all the US states where voters elect their utility regulators. These include burgeoning data center hubs Arizona and Georgia. Governors will be chosen in 36 US states this year, and governors appoint utility regulators in states where commissioners are not directly elected.  In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton has promised to lower energy bills if she is elected governor. Her campaign said she will also appoint a public utilities commission that was "not beholden to utility companies" and work with the state attorney general to crack down on "excessive rate hikes and predatory practices." Ohio's residential electricity bills have grown by more than 20 per cent over the last two years, according to EIA data. Acton has also said she supports a data center moratorium. Her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy said he would assure Ohioans living near data centers would not pay electricity bills at all. BULLY PULPIT Some governors who are up for reelection have used their political weight to pressure the power industry to keep prices down. In April, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro announced that prominent utility, PECO Energy Company, had acceded to his demand that it withdraw its proposal with state regulators to increase rates. Shapiro, a Democrat running for reelection, said the move would reduce future utility bills by as much as $34 a month. He followed up with a letter to more utility CEOs seeking changes in how utilities justify spending and returns on equity. "The governors are using this crisis on energy affordability as an opportunity to take a deeper dive into the utility regulatory model and see if it makes any sense," said Jamie Van Nostrand, senior fellow at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy at the University of Pennsylvania and former chair of the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities.  Power bills tracked low inflation for roughly a decade, and were not an issue in most mainstream elections until last year, when Mikie Sherrill successfully ran for New Jersey governor on the promise of freezing utility bills. She did so the same day she took office. In Virginia, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world, Governor Abigail Spanberger took a similar approach, which industry analysts said could offer a playbook for those who win this year’s elections.  Utility advocates say reducing guaranteed returns and freezing rates will not make a meaningful difference in household bills but could lead to a long-term reduction of investments in the grid. "The grid is America's greatest machine, and it doesn't operate on the political calendar,” said Drew Maloney, president of Edison Electric Institute, a trade organization for investor-owned electric utilities. “It requires consistent investment every year to deliver reliable energy to our customers." Credit rating agency Fitch downgraded the North American utility sector to "deteriorating" from "neutral" in June, citing political pressure in the midterms to limit electricity bills and utility profits. For an industry that plans in decades, it is hard to predict the result of short-term political moves aimed at saving money for households. "I do think the real meat will come after the election," Hua said.

Source: Reuters
